title: Why compressed files sometimes get bigger
description: An efficient file may have little room to shrink. Learn why compression can retain the original, and how conversions and resizing differ.
seoDescription: Understand real file-size savings, original-retained 0% results, and why an explicit format conversion or resize may produce a larger output.

body.text: A file may already be efficiently encoded for the quality you need. Re-encoding it can produce little benefit or a larger candidate. A smaller file is useful only if its dimensions, format and visible quality still suit the job.
A percentage alone can be confusing. Compare actual byte counts and the result label: smaller, original retained, larger transformation, or target not met.

body.caption: Illustrative size outcomes, not measured benchmarks. Ordinary compression retains the original when no smaller candidate is found.

body.text: The following examples illustrate reporting rather than product performance. Savings are calculated from the actual input and output bytes, not a promised compression percentage.

items: Smaller: an output below the original size provides a real, measurable reduction. Inspect quality as well as bytes before keeping it.
Original retained: an ordinary compression candidate that is not smaller is discarded. The unchanged original has 0% reduction and retains its existing metadata.
Larger transformation: a requested format conversion, resize or new ZIP archive can increase bytes. Growth is labelled larger rather than as a saving.

body.text: Compression and conversion have different goals

Ordinary same-format compression tries to reduce file size while keeping the format and default dimensions. FileCompresser keeps the original if the candidate is not smaller. Explicitly choosing another format is a conversion, and a different encoding can require more bytes.

Resizing is also a separate choice. Image dimensions are preserved unless you enable resizing. A smaller image may save bytes by containing fewer pixels; that change should never be hidden inside a compression preset.
A maximum-size target is a separate requirement

Target size verifies the actual byte count against your maximum. A result over the limit is marked Target not met. A target does not authorize silent resizing, and a valid output alone does not mean the requested size was achieved.

body.title: The rule
body.text: Never present growth as a saving. Keep the original when ordinary compression cannot reduce it, and clearly describe larger transformations or an unmet target.

Review the downloaded file, not just a thumbnail or a percentage. Check dimensions, format, transparency, text readability, playback and byte counts. A retained original is unchanged, including its metadata; an encoded result can remove metadata or normalize color. Keep your source until you have verified the result.
